titleText.es: Aparentemente, Google asume que viajarás durante las horas operativas del ferry. Perdimos dos horas rodeando ese maldito lago (por no hablar del Hombre de Paja).
titleText.en: Apparently Google assumes you're traveling during the ferry's normal operating hours. We lost two hours circling that damn lake (to say nothing of the Straw Man).
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive closely follows the official English title text and translates Straw Man literally as Hombre de Paja.

cards.answerEn: through; along; down; via (a movement path)
cards.noteEn: Por can mark the path followed during movement. English may choose through, along, down, or via according to the route.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone starts doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of empezar, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign means “followed by.” The dictionary form, also called the infinitive, is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Empezar changes for the person and time; a stays fixed, and the action verb stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)
to cause; to give (in dar problemas)
cards.noteEn: Dar usually means “to give.” In dar problemas, English naturally uses “cause” or “create” instead.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something causes trouble or creates problems?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of dar followed by problema or problemas.
cards.noteEn: Dar literally means “to give,” but dar problemas is the conventional way to say that something causes trouble. Dar changes for the person, thing, and time; problemas stays a noun.
Before a number or amount of time, como can show that the amount is approximate rather than exact.
Before a place in a sequence, por can mark an approximate position rather than a route or cause.

example.es: La explicación aparece por la página diez.
example.en: The explanation appears around page ten.

cards.answerEn: by; from (identifying the creator or source)
cards.noteEn: De can connect a work, statement, or piece of commentary to the person who created or supplied it. Natural English often uses “by” rather than literal “of.”

example.en: I read an article by Marta.

cards.noteEn: Gira tells one familiar person to turn. It comes from girar, “to turn.”

cards.promptEs: girar a la izquierda / a la derecha
cards.questionEn: How do you tell someone to turn left or right?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of girar, then a la izquierda for left or a la derecha for right.
cards.noteEn: Only girar changes for the person and time. The directional part stays a la izquierda or a la derecha; the a is part of this standard navigation expression.

example.es: Gira a la derecha en la esquina.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
Continúa tells one familiar person to continue. The written accent keeps the stress on ú.

cards.answerEn: take (a form of transport; informal command)
cards.noteEn: Toma tells one familiar person to use or board the named transport. It comes from tomar.
Ferry is a borrowed noun used in Spanish for a boat that carries passengers or vehicles across water.

example.es: El ferry sale a las nueve.

cards.noteEn: Atraviesa tells one familiar person to cross something from one side to the other.
Before a place, hasta marks the endpoint reached by movement. English often uses simply to, while as far as makes the endpoint emphasis explicit.

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”

cards.noteEn: With a vehicle or service, tomar means using it to travel.

example.en: We are going to take the train.

cards.answerEn: it is (in an impersonal time expression)
cards.noteEn: Spanish can use es without a separate subject word in expressions such as es hora, “it is time.” English supplies the impersonal word “it.”

cards.answerEn: past; later than (with a stated time)
cards.noteEn: Más normally means “more.” In a time expression such as es más de medianoche, it says the stated time has already passed.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links más to the time already passed
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses más de before the stated time; English can express the whole combination with “past.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something is scary or frightens someone?
cards.answerEn: Name the scary thing, use the matching form of dar, and add miedo. Use me, te, le, nos, os, or les when you need to name who feels afraid.
cards.noteEn: Spanish presents the source of fear as “giving fear.” Dar changes for that source; miedo stays unchanged. The small person marker identifies who feels the fear and can be omitted for a general statement.
Da is a present form of dar. With a feeling such as miedo, English normally uses “causes,” “makes ... feel,” or a verb such as “scares.”
Guiaría combines guiar with the -ía ending to describe what someone or something would do.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.
After estar, mal can describe something as wrong, incorrect, or not as it should be. English uses the adjective ‘wrong,’ even though mal often works like an adverb in Spanish.
Déjame joins the affirmative command deja, “let,” to me, which marks the person receiving permission. The accent keeps the original stress after the pronoun is attached.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone lets another person do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dejar, mark the person receiving permission with me, te, le, nos, os, or les, and put the allowed action in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged dictionary form is the verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The person marker can stand before a changed form of dejar, join an affirmative command such as déjame, or in some structures join the following dictionary-form verb. Dejar changes for the person and time; the allowed action does not.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.noteEn: Trepa tells one familiar person to climb. It comes from trepar.
Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.answerEn: hanged man; person executed by hanging
cards.noteEn: Ahorcado comes from ahorcar, “to hang by the neck.” As a noun it can name a person who has been hanged.

example.es: La leyenda habla de un ahorcado.
example.en: The legend tells of a hanged man.

cards.noteEn: Evitando is evitar with the -ando ending, which presents the avoiding as accompanying another action.

example.es: Cruzó la plaza evitando la lluvia.
example.en: She crossed the square while avoiding the rain.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

cards.promptEs: cuando + presente de subjuntivo para un hecho futuro
cards.questionEn: After cuando, how do you describe an event that has not happened yet?
cards.answerEn: Use cuando followed by a present subjunctive form for the future event; put the main result in an ordinary future or command form.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used here because the time of the future event is not yet a fact. For example, mover changes to mueva. Spanish does not normally put a future-tense form immediately after cuando in this pattern.

example.en: I will call you when I arrive.

cards.answerEn: you arrive; you reach (special form for an event still ahead)
cards.noteEn: Llegues is a present subjunctive form of llegar. After cuando, it presents the arrival as a future event that has not happened yet.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Ve is the irregular positive command of ir for one familiar person. It is different from ve meaning “he or she sees.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links an item to atrás to describe it as the back or rear one
cards.noteEn: Spanish can put de atrás after an object to identify the one positioned at the back. Natural English usually puts “back” before the noun.

cards.answerEn: knock (on a door; informal singular command)
cards.noteEn: Llamar usually means “to call.” In llamar a la puerta, it means knocking so that someone answers.

example.es: Llama a la puerta antes de entrar.
example.en: Knock on the door before entering.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone knocks on a door?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of llamar followed by a la puerta.
cards.noteEn: Llamar usually means “to call,” but llamar a la puerta is the conventional expression for knocking on a door. Only llamar changes for the person and time; a la puerta stays unchanged unless a different door is named.

cards.answerEn: on; fixed link in llamar a la puerta
cards.noteEn: This a belongs to the conventional expression llamar a la puerta, “to knock on the door.” It is not marking movement toward a destination.

cards.promptEs: número ordinal antes de un sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you use words such as first, second, or third before a Spanish noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the ordinal before the noun and make its ending match the noun's gender and number.
cards.noteEn: An ordinal gives a position in an order. Primero, segundo, tercero, último, and similar words usually come before the noun. Most forms use -o with a masculine singular noun and -a with a feminine singular noun, but primero and tercero shorten to primer and tercer before a masculine singular noun. Plural nouns use plural forms.

example.es: La segunda puerta está en el tercer piso.
example.en: The second door is on the third floor.

cards.noteEn: Pregunta tells one familiar person to ask. With por, it means asking to speak to or find someone.

cards.questionEn: How do you ask to speak to, see, or find a particular person?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of preguntar, then por, then the person.
cards.noteEn: Preguntar alone means “to ask.” Preguntar por alguien conventionally means asking for that person or asking where that person is. Preguntar changes for the person and time; por stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: for; required after preguntar before the person sought
cards.noteEn: Preguntar por alguien means asking to speak to, see, or locate that person.

cards.answerEn: tell him/her; say to him/her (informal singular command)
cards.noteEn: Dile joins the command di, from decir, to le, which marks the person receiving the message.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cards.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, then use a phrase beginning with the word a to identify the receiver explicitly.
cards.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once. In the prompt, the slash means that le and les are alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and the named receiver.
Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.
Danzante can describe a person or thing that dances.

cards.answerEn: they rest; they are at rest

cards.noteEn: Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.
Dará is the future form of dar used with one person or thing.

example.en: Ana will give you the key.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
Su agrees with the possessed thing, not with the owner. The same Spanish form can mean his, her, its, their, or formal your; the surrounding context identifies the owner.
As a warning by itself, cuidado means “careful” or “watch out.”

cards.answerEn: go down; travel down (informal singular command)
cards.noteEn: Baja tells one familiar person to move downward or along a descending route.
Here mina is the place where minerals are extracted, not the explosive device.

cards.answerEn: belonging to; often expressed with ’s in English
cards.noteEn: De can connect a thing to its owner. Spanish says el libro de Ana where English can say ‘Ana’s book.’

cards.promptEs: orden negativa de tú: no + verbo
cards.questionEn: How do you tell one friend or familiar person not to do something?
cards.answerEn: Put no before the verb's special negative-command form. If the verb uses te, put te between no and the verb.
cards.noteEn: For a regular -ar verb, the negative form usually ends in -es: hablar becomes no hables. Regular -er and -ir verbs usually end in -as: comer becomes no comas. A short word such as te goes before this negative form, as in no te levantes.

cards.answerEn: wake up (special form in a negative informal command)
cards.noteEn: Despiertes is the special tú form used after no to tell one familiar person not to wake up. Despertarse uses te with that person, so the complete command places te before the verb: no te despiertes.

cards.answerEn: a + el before a specific person; often “the” or “to the” in English
cards.noteEn: Spanish contracts a + el to al. The personal a can mark a specific person who receives or is affected by an action; English may use “the,” “to the,” or no separate preposition, depending on the verb.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Espantapájaros combines a form related to espantar, “to scare away,” with pájaros, “birds.” The compound has the same form in singular and plural.

example.es: Hay un espantapájaros en el campo.
example.en: There is a scarecrow in the field.

cards.answerEn: you feel (special form for an event still ahead)
cards.noteEn: Sientas is a present subjunctive form of sentir. After cuando, it presents the feeling as a future event that has not happened yet.

cards.answerEn: your here; Spanish keeps “the” because te already marks the affected owner
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses an article before a body part when me, te, le, nos, or les already identifies whose body is affected.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone's blood runs cold from fear?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of helarse with la sangre, and use me, te, le, nos, os, or les to mark the person who feels the fear.
cards.noteEn: Helar literally means “to freeze.” Se makes it helarse, where the blood itself goes cold, and the person marker identifies whose reaction it is. The form of helar changes for the time; sangre is singular, so the verb is singular.

example.es: Al oír el grito, se me heló la sangre.
example.en: When I heard the scream, my blood ran cold.

cards.promptEs: verbo + el/la/los/las + parte del cuerpo (dueño claro)
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes use the word for “the” before a body part where English uses “my,” “your,” or “their”?
cards.answerEn: When the context already makes the owner clear, Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las before the body part instead of a possessive word such as mi or tu.
cards.noteEn: Choose el, la, los, or las to match the body part, not its owner: la mano is feminine singular, while los brazos is masculine plural. The verb or another short word in context can identify whose body part it is. If the owner would not otherwise be clear, Spanish can still use a possessive word.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks helarse, “to freeze” or “go cold”
cards.noteEn: The small word se turns helar, “to freeze something,” into helarse, where the subject itself freezes or goes cold.

cards.answerEn: marks you as the affected owner; English often uses “your”
cards.noteEn: Spanish can identify an affected owner with me, te, le, nos, or les and still use el or la before the owned thing. English often uses a possessive instead: te rompieron el móvil means “they broke your phone.”
Hiela is a present form of helar. The e changes to ie in this form.

example.es: El lago se hiela en invierno.

cards.questionEn: Why does a verb such as cerrar change its middle e to ie in forms such as cierras?
cards.answerEn: For certain verbs, change the stressed e in the verb's base to ie in most present-time forms.
cards.noteEn: The stressed e is the e in the syllable you naturally pronounce most strongly. The base is what remains after removing -ar, -er, or -ir. Cerrar has the base cerr-, which becomes cierr- in cierro, cierras, cierra, and cierran. The forms for nosotros and vosotros keep e: cerramos and cerráis. Only some e verbs follow this pattern, so learn the change with each verb.

cards.answerEn: your here; Spanish uses “the” before body parts whose owner is already clear
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly keeps the article before a body part and lets the surrounding pronoun or context identify the owner.
Detén is the command form of detener used with one familiar person. It takes a written accent.
Sal is the irregular command form of salir for one familiar person.
Quédate joins the command queda to te because the verb is quedarse, “to stay.” The accent preserves the original stress.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone remains in, or ends up in, a particular state?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of quedarse followed by a word that names the resulting or continuing state.
cards.noteEn: The plus sign in the prompt means that the state word follows quedarse. Quedarse is pronominal: it comes with me, te, se, nos, or os even though no one literally remains themselves. Change quedar and its small marker to match the person and time. When another verb has already changed for the person, the marker may stand before that verb: se puede quedar.

example.es: Después de la noticia, Pablo se quedó callado.
example.en: After the news, Pablo fell silent.

cards.answerEn: they are (in a place or state)

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.
Without a following noun, este can name the cardinal direction east; this is different from este meaning “this.”

example.es: El sol sale por el este.
example.en: The sun rises in the east.

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.
The -as ending matches a feminine plural noun.

The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the person or thing feared with temerle
cards.noteEn: In varieties that use temerle a, le appears with the verb and a introduces the feared target.

example.en: He is afraid of the dark.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is afraid of a particular person or thing using temerle?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of temer with le or les, then a before the person or thing that is feared.
cards.noteEn: In varieties that use this pattern, le or les appears with temer and a introduces the feared target. Temer changes for who feels the fear; le or les matches the target as singular or plural. Other varieties also use temer directly without le and a.

example.en: Marta is afraid of the dog.

cards.noteEn: Teme is a present form of temer used with one person or thing.

cards.answerEn: of; combines a + el before what is feared after temerle
cards.noteEn: In temerle a algo, the required a combines with el to form al before a masculine singular target.
Equipo can also mean equipment; here it names a group of people working together.

example.en: The team is looking for a solution.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.
Ayudarte joins ayudar, “to help,” to te, “you.” Spanish writes the two pieces as one word.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.answerEn: anymore; any longer (after a negative verb)
cards.noteEn: Más usually means ‘more.’ After no and a verb, it can instead reinforce that an action no longer happens, especially in Latin American usage.

example.en: I do not work there anymore.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what will happen if a real possibility occurs?
cards.answerEn: Use si with an ordinary present-time verb form for the condition, then state the result with a future form.
cards.noteEn: Si introduces a condition treated as genuinely possible. Spanish normally keeps the verb immediately after si in the present form, not the future. The result can use the future, built here by keeping the action verb and adding an ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.

example.en: If you finish early, we will have dinner together.

cards.noteEn: Dominas is the ordinary present form of dominar for one familiar person.
Guiará combines the unchanged verb guiar with the -á future ending for one person or thing.
At the start of a stand-alone wish, que introduces the hoped-for event and is followed by a special subjunctive verb form.

cards.questionEn: How do you express a stand-alone hope or wish for someone?
cards.answerEn: Begin with que, name who or what the wish concerns, and use a special subjunctive form for the hoped-for action.
cards.noteEn: The subjunctive is a special verb form used here because the event is wished for rather than stated as fact. For example, tener changes to tengas and ayudar changes to ayude. This stand-alone que does not need a preceding verb meaning “I hope.”

example.en: May you have a good trip.

cards.noteEn: Ayude is a present subjunctive form of ayudar. After wish-introducing que, it presents the helping as something hoped for.
